t.6.1: Then Gaurī privately sent word through her friend to the Soul of the Universe: "Let the lord of the mountains, who is the one to give me away, be made the authority."
t.6.3: Having promised, "So be it," and having with difficulty let Umā go, he, the chastiser of Smara, called to mind the seven Ṛṣis, made of light.
t.6.2: Her message having been spoken for her by her friend, she shone, O dear one, modest and silent, like a slender mango branch that speaks through the mouth of a cuckoo when spring is near.
t.6.4: Those ascetics, rich in penance, illuminating the sky with their circles of radiance, appeared at once before the Lord, together with Arundhatī.
t.6.5: They had bathed in the streams of the Ākāśagaṅgā, whose waves scatter the mandāra blossoms from its banks and whose waters are fragrant with the rut-fluid of the elephants of the quarters.
t.6.6: Wearing sacred threads of pearls, clad in garments of golden bark and bearing rosaries of jewels, they looked like wish-granting trees that had taken up the life of wandering ascetics.
t.6.7: They were ever gazed up at with due reverence by the thousand-rayed Sun, who turned his horses downward and lowered his banner before them.
t.6.8: In the calamity of the cosmic dissolution, they rested upon the tusk of the Great Boar together with the uplifted Earth, whose creeper-like arms clung to it.
t.6.9: Because they carried out the remainder of creation immediately after the Womb of the universe, these ancient ones are celebrated as Creators by those who know the lore of old.
t.6.11: Standing in their midst, the virtuous Arundhatī, her eyes fixed upon her husband's feet, shone brilliantly, like the very embodiment of the perfection of austerity.
t.6.10: Even while enjoying the fruits of their former pure austerities, which had come to full ripeness, they still remained ascetics.
t.6.12: The Lord looked upon her and upon the sages with no difference in reverence. Whether one is a woman or a man is of no concern, for it is conduct that is honored by the good.
t.6.13: At the sight of her, Śambhu's longing for a wife grew stronger, for virtuous wives are indeed the very root and means of all righteous rites.
t.6.15: Then all those sages, deeply learned in the Veda, their skin bristling with joy, having paid honor to the Teacher of the world, spoke these words.
t.6.14: When Śarva had been made to take a step toward Pārvatī, even though it was Dharma that moved him, the mind of Kāma, still fearful because of his former offense, breathed again with relief.
t.6.16: The Veda that we have duly recited, the offerings we have poured into the fire according to rule, and the austerity we have practised: today the fruit of all that has ripened for us.
t.6.17: That you, the overseer of the worlds, have raised us to a place in your own mind, a height beyond the reach of even our wishes...
t.6.18: He in whose mind you would dwell is already the foremost of the accomplished; how much more, then, is he who dwells in the mind of you, the very source of Brahmā!
t.6.19: Truly, we occupy a station beyond the Sun and the Moon; but today, through that favor of your remembering us, we stand higher still.
t.6.20: Honored by you, we now think highly of ourselves; for, as a rule, the regard of the most exalted instills confidence in one's own virtues.
t.6.21: O Virūpākṣa, the joy that has arisen in us from your thinking of us, why should it be told to you? You are the inner self of all embodied beings.
t.6.22: You are seen by us face to face, yet we do not truly know you. Be gracious and tell us of yourself, for you do not dwell within the path of thought.
t.6.23: Is it that by which you create the manifest world, or that by which you sustain it, or else the destroyer of the universe? Which part of you is this?
t.6.24: Or rather, O God, let this exceedingly great request rest. For now, command us, who have come the moment you thought of us: what shall we do?
t.6.25: Then the Supreme Lord replied, augmenting the faint radiance of the moon resting upon his crest with the bright rays of his teeth.
t.6.26: It is known to you that none of my activities are undertaken for my own sake; am I not, indeed, revealed to be of such a nature by my eight forms?
t.6.27: Such as I am, I have been entreated for offspring by the gods, harassed by their enemies, just as the lightning-bearing cloud is entreated for rain by the cātaka birds tormented by thirst.
t.6.28: Therefore I wish to obtain Pārvatī for the sake of a son born of myself, just as a sacrificer seeks the araṇi fire-stick for the kindling of the fire, the eater of oblations.
t.6.29: Himālaya must be asked by you for her hand on my behalf; for alliances arranged through the good never turn to ill.
t.6.30: Know that I too am not shortchanged in being joined in kinship with him, the lofty and steadfast one who bears the burden of the earth.
t.6.31: No instruction is given to you on how he should be addressed on behalf of the maiden, for the virtuous hold as sacred the conduct laid down by you yourselves.
t.6.32: The noble Arundhatī too ought to take part in that matter, for in an affair of this kind it is, as a rule, matrons who show assurance and skill.
t.6.33: Therefore go, for the success of this purpose, to Oṣadhiprastha, the city of Himavat; and our meeting again shall be right here, at this waterfall of the Mahākośī.
t.6.34: When he, the foremost of the self-restrained, had become eager for marriage, the ascetics descended from Prajāpati cast off their shame at having taken wives.
t.6.35: Then, having said “So be it,” the circle of sages set out; and the Blessed One too reached the place that had first been appointed.
t.6.36: And those supreme seers, swift as thought itself, flew up into the sky, dark as a sword-blade, and arrived at Oṣadhiprastha.
t.6.37: It seemed to have been founded as if it had outdone Alakā, the dwelling-place of abundant riches, and as if it had been made an outlet for the overflow of heaven.
t.6.38: A city whose rampart was built of huge slabs of jewel-stone, delightful to the heart even in its defenses.
t.6.39: There the elephants have overcome their fear of lions, the horses are born of caverns, the citizens are Yakṣas and Kiṃpuruṣas, and the women are goddesses of the forest.
t.6.40: There, in the mansions whose peaks have clouds clinging to them, the sounds of the muraja drums, made uncertain by the answering thunder, can be told apart only by their rhythmic strokes.
t.6.41: Where the splendor of banners on the houses' flagstaffs is fashioned not by the citizens' care but by the wish-granting trees themselves, with silken garments fluttering on their swaying branches.
t.6.43: Where women going to meet their lovers by night, their paths revealed by the glow of luminous herbs, know nothing of darkness even on stormy days.
t.6.42: There, at night, on the drinking-terraces of the crystal mansions, the reflections of the stars become offerings, like flowers strewn for the revellers.
t.6.44: There, age ends only in youth, the only affliction is the flower-weaponed god of love, and the only loss of consciousness is the sleep that arises from the weariness of lovemaking.
t.6.45: There the women's fits of anger, with knitted brows, quivering lips and the graceful threatening of a finger, turned their lovers into suppliants pleading for their favor.
t.6.46: And whose outer pleasure-grove is fragrant Gandhamādana, where Vidyādhara wayfarers lie asleep in the shade of the saṃtānaka trees.
t.6.47: Then those divine sages, beholding the city of Himālaya, regarded the merit they had earned with heaven as its aim as little more than a deception.
t.6.48: Watched by the doorkeepers with upturned faces, they swiftly descended upon the mountain's mansion, their masses of matted hair as motionless as fire painted in a picture.
t.6.49: That line of sages, descending from the sky with the eldest leading in order of seniority, shone like a row of suns gleaming within the water.
t.6.50: Taking up the guest-offering, the Mountain went out from afar to meet those worthy of honor, bending the earth beneath steps heavy with the weight of his mass.
t.6.51: With his lower lip coppery-red like mineral ore, towering in height, his mighty arms like deodar trees, and his chest by its very nature broad as rock, he was plainly recognizable as Himavān.
t.6.53: There, the mountain, bearer of the earth, having himself taken a seat, with hands joined in reverence, spoke these words to the lords seated on cane seats.
t.6.52: He himself showing them the way, he led into the inner palace those sages of pure deeds, who had been honored with hospitality offered according to rule.
t.6.54: The sight of you, come about beyond all expectation, appears to me like rain arising without clouds, like fruit whose blossom was never seen.
t.6.55: By your grace I regard myself, though dull, as if awakened; though made of iron, as if turned to gold; as if I had risen from the earth to heaven.
t.6.56: From this day forth I am to be approached by beings for their purification, for whatever place has been dwelt upon by the worthy, that, they declare, is a tīrtha.
t.6.57: O best of the twice-born, I consider myself purified by just two things: by the fall of the Gaṅgā upon my head, and by the water that has washed your feet.
t.6.58: Though my body is twofold, the moving form engaged in your service and the stationary form marked by your feet, I consider it to have received your favor shared between both.
t.6.59: My limbs, though they stretch to the ends of the directions, are not enough to hold the swelling joy that springs from the honor you have shown me.
t.6.60: By the sight of you, radiant ones, not only has the darkness dwelling in my caves been dispelled, but also the darkness within me, which lies even beyond passion.
t.6.61: I see nothing that you need to have done; and if there were, what would not be readily accomplished? I suspect that your journey here is solely for my purification.
t.6.62: Even so, you should give me a command in some matter, for servants count being put to use as a favor from their mighty masters.
t.6.64: Having spoken thus, Himālaya uttered that very meaning as if a second time, through the echo spreading forth from the mouths of his caves.
t.6.63: Here we are, here is my wife, and here is this maiden, the very life of our family; tell us which of these you have need of here, for we hold no regard for external things.
t.6.65: Then the sages urged Aṅgiras, the foremost among them in matters of eloquent speech, and he gave his reply to the mountain.
t.6.66: All this, and even more than this, is fitting in you; the loftiness of your mind is equal to that of your peaks.
t.6.67: Fittingly do they call you Viṣṇu in immovable form, and rightly so, for your belly has become the support of all beings, moving and unmoving.
t.6.68: How could the serpent have upheld the earth with his hoods, soft as lotus stalks, had you not supported it from the very depths of Rasātala?
t.6.69: Your glories and your rivers, their pure continuous streams unbroken and unchecked even by the ocean's waves, purify the worlds through their holiness.
t.6.70: Just as Gaṅgā is glorified by the foot of Parameṣṭhin, her source, so too is she glorified by you, her second source, whose head rises high.
t.6.71: The greatness of Hari, pervading across, above and below, was his only when he rose up to take his three strides; but that same greatness is natural to you.
t.6.72: By you, who have attained a lofty station in the midst of those who enjoy shares of the sacrifice, the golden peak of Sumeru has been rendered vain.
t.6.73: All hardness has been placed by you in your immovable body; but this form of yours, bowed low with devotion, is given to honouring the good.
t.6.74: Hear, then, the purpose of our coming; that purpose is truly yours alone. Yet because we counsel what is good, we too have a share in it.
t.6.75: He who bears on high, together with the crescent moon, the title 'Īśvara', which is endowed with the powers beginning with minuteness and has never touched any other being.
t.6.76: He by whom, through earth and the other elements, whose powers are fitted to support one another, this whole universe is upheld within himself, as a carriage is borne along the road by its yoked beasts of burden.
t.6.77: He whom yogins seek as the one dwelling within the field of the body, whose abode the wise declare to be free from the fear of return to rebirth.
t.6.78: That Śambhu, the giver of boons, the witness of every deed in the universe, himself seeks your daughter in marriage through words conveyed by us.
t.6.79: You ought to unite him with your daughter, as meaning is united with speech; for a daughter given to a good husband is not to be grieved over by her father.
t.6.81: Having bowed to Śitikaṇṭha, the gods immediately afterward color her feet with the rays of the jewels in their crests.
t.6.80: So that all these beings, both the stationary and the moving, may regard her as their mother, for the Lord is the father of the world.
t.6.82: Umā is the bride, you are the giver, and we here are the ones who ask; Śambhu is the bridegroom. Surely this arrangement is enough to exalt your family.
t.6.83: Through the bond of giving your daughter in marriage, become the elder of the world's elder, of him who praises no one yet is himself praised, who is worthy of homage yet bows to no other.
t.6.84: While the divine sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing at her father's side with her face cast down, counted the petals of the lotus she held in play.
t.6.85: Though his own wish was wholly fulfilled, the Mountain looked to Menā's face, for in matters concerning a daughter, householders generally see through the eyes of their wives.
t.6.86: Menā too regarded all that her husband desired as what must be done. Wives devoted to their husbands never deviate from what their lord wishes.
t.6.87: Reflecting in his mind, “This is the fitting answer here,” he, at the end of their words, took hold of his daughter, adorned with auspicious ornaments.
t.6.88: Come, my child, you have been destined as alms for the Self of the universe. The sages are the petitioners, and by me the fruit of the householder's life has been attained.
t.6.89: Having said only this much to his daughter, the Mountain said to the sages: “This bride of the Three-eyed One bows to you all.”
t.6.90: Having welcomed the mountain's words, generous in accomplishing the end they sought, they made Ambikā flourish with blessings whose fulfillment was close at hand.
t.6.91: Arundhatī lifted her onto her lap, the bashful maiden whose golden ear-ornament had slipped down as she bowed in reverence.
t.6.92: And she freed from grief that girl's mother, whose face was wet with tears and who was distraught with love for her daughter, by telling of the virtues of the bridegroom, who had never belonged to any other before.
t.6.93: Asked at that very moment by Hara's kinsman about the day of the wedding, the bark-clad sages declared it to be three days hence and departed.
t.6.94: Taking leave of Himālaya, they went back to Śūlin, and when they had reported to him that his purpose was accomplished, they were dismissed by him and rose up into the sky.
t.6.95: Even Paśupati, eager for union with the Mountain's Daughter, passed those days only with difficulty; whom else, helpless, would these emotions not torment, since they touch even him, the all-pervading Lord?
